title: The ten words, part two (Exodus 20:12–17)
hookLine: honor parents, no murder, adultery, stealing, lying or coveting
tomorrow: The stranger, the widow, the orphan

cards: Picture an ordinary street. A teenager rolling her eyes at her dad. A man at a bar, angry enough to swing.
A couple drifting toward an affair over text. A cashier slipping a twenty into his pocket. Someone giving the police a statement that bends the truth.

And a neighbor staring over the fence at a nicer car, a bigger house, and feeling something sour rise. Six scenes, and every one is covered by the second half of the ten words. The first half turned toward God.
Now the voice on the mountain turns to the people next door.

teach.h: HONOR PARENTS: A COMMAND WITH A PROMISE.
teach.b: It starts at home, in the King James Bible: "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee."
Centuries later, in his letter to the Ephesians, Paul calls it the first commandment with a promise.
Then come three commands so short they're almost blunt: "Thou shalt not kill. Thou shalt not commit adultery. Thou shalt not steal." In Hebrew each is just two words. Lo tirtzach.
Lo tinaf. Lo tignov. The verb in lo tirtzach is usually used for unlawful killing, which is why many modern translations say murder.
The law elsewhere still deals with war and capital cases, so readers have argued over its edges for centuries.
Then, no false witness against your neighbor: in a world with no cameras, a lie in court could cost someone their life.

teach.h: THE LAST ONE IS ABOUT WANTING.
teach.b: And the last one is different from all the rest.
Thou shalt not covet: your neighbor's house, spouse, servants, ox, donkey, anything that is your neighbor's. Every other command is about something you do. This one is about something you want.

It reaches inside. You could keep the other nine perfectly and still break the tenth in your own kitchen, staring out the window. Christians often hear the two halves as two tables: love of God, and love of neighbor.
Jesus, asked for the greatest commandment, gave an answer with exactly that shape. More on that in a couple of weeks.

how: Many Christians use the Ten Commandments to examine their conscience, especially before confession or communion, and churches teach them in catechism classes as the shape of love for God and neighbor.

games.q: you've kept nine of the ten perfectly. then you stare over the fence at your neighbor's life, and want it. which word have you broken?
games.why: the tenth word is about wanting. it's the only one you can break without lifting a finger.

practice: Walk slowly down the list in your mind, honor parents, no killing, no adultery, no stealing, no false witness, no coveting, and notice which one catches a little: the parent you haven't called, a small exaggeration about a coworker, the scrolling that leaves you wanting someone else's life.
Picture keeping that one, on purpose, just for today. If you pray, you can ask for help with it.

wordCard.voice: Lo tirtzach. Hebrew for thou shalt not kill, from a verb usually meaning unlawful killing, one of the ten words carved for neighbor and self.
